name: Salacia
short: Small, short trials only: Salacia drink raised breath hydrogen, mild flatulence; prediabetes: no adverse events (6 wk), no meaningful safety concerns (12 wk); diabetes tea trial: events not listed.
text: Human safety data on Salacia come from small, short trials of extracts taken by mouth, using several species. A 2015 review stated that no adverse effects were reported in human studies of Salacia extracts and that studies in rats and mice of Salacia reticulata, Salacia oblonga and Salacia chinensis indicated the extracts were exceedingly safe. In a 6-week randomised placebo-controlled trial of Salacia reticulata leaf and root bark extracts in 29 people with prediabetes and raised blood lipids, no adverse events occurred and all safety parameters stayed within normal ranges; in a 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trial of a Salacia reticulata extract in 100 adults with prediabetes, no clinically meaningful safety concerns were observed; and in a single-dose crossover study of Salacia chinensis extract in 35 healthy volunteers, no significant adverse events were observed. In a randomised crossover trial in 51 people with type 2 diabetes who drank a herbal tea containing Salacia reticulata for 3 months, liver and kidney function and adverse events were monitored and the authors concluded the tea was effective and safe; the abstract does not list any adverse events. The same abstract reports that the daily mean dose of the diabetes medicine glibenclamide fell by 1.89 mg in the tea-treated group but rose by 2.25 mg in the placebo-treated group (P = 0.07), and that differences in metformin dose between the two groups were not statistically significant; it does not say why the doses changed. In 43 healthy adults given a liquid nutritional drink containing Salacia oblonga extract, with or without two added amino acids, breath hydrogen excretion was 60% greater with the Salacia-containing meals and was associated with mild flatulence. Apart from the dose changes in the tea trial, the cited sources give no data on interactions with medicines.
